segments.title: Battleship autoloaders need fire-control context
segments.body: Ideas for mechanically assisted loading of battleship-calibre guns appeared well before modern digital systems. A very large shell still demands a workable fire-control solution, because rapid salvo fire is of little use if the ship cannot obtain accurate range information. Radar direction and a fire-control computer make a small number of carefully aimed shots more credible than repeated ranging salvos. Any armour practical on a ship would be hard pressed to defeat a functioning 24-inch armour-piercing shell.

evidence.note: The panel discusses historic autoloader research, radar-directed gunnery, armour, and very large shells.

segments.summary: A speculative 24-inch autoloader leads to a practical discussion of why rapid heavy-gun fire needs radar-directed fire control and realistic protection for the loading system.

segments.title: Why splashdown recovery needs maritime engineering
segments.body: A hardpoint designed for controlled lifting may be poorly suited to towing through the open ocean. An attachment can be strong enough for a recovery arm yet sit in the wrong place relative to the vehicle's buoyancy when current, waves, and towline forces act on it. Salvage specialists and naval architects should test those assumptions before they become fixed in the design. Salt-water exposure also complicates a rapid-reuse concept. Expertise in aerospace structures does not automatically cover maritime recovery.

evidence.note: The panel compares controlled lifting with open-ocean towing and discusses buoyancy, salvage expertise, naval architecture, and salt-water exposure.

segments.summary: Starship recovery prompts a practical warning that lifting points, towing loads, buoyancy, sea state, and salt-water exposure are different engineering problems.

segments.title: Matching Star Wars roles to real naval command skills
segments.body: Fictional command posts correspond to different real-world jobs, so fame alone does not identify the best admiral for each role. Jackie Fisher is proposed for a Tarkin-like position because it combines policy, construction, doctrine, and institutional reform. Collingwood represents a commander who wins by denying an enemy supplies and options before battle, while Rochefort represents intelligence-led anticipation of an opponent's decisions. Billy Mitchell's outsider campaign for reform required a different kind of political skill.

evidence.note: Historical candidates are compared with Tarkin and Thrawn through policy, logistics, intelligence, and reform.

segments.question: Which historical naval figures would best replace Imperial leaders such as Tarkin and Thrawn?
segments.answerShort: Fisher suits institutional transformation, while tacticians such as Collingwood and intelligence specialists such as Rochefort represent the skills associated with Thrawn.

segments.title: Judge Fletcher's carrier decision with the information he had
segments.body: Claims that Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher was a coward overlook the information and operational risks behind his disputed Pacific carrier decision. Fletcher made a sensible choice from the information available, even though that information was wrong and US Marines were left without nearby carriers. Carrier aviation did not require the hulls themselves to remain fixed next to the landing area because aircraft could fly from a safer position. Keeping fleet carriers close could expose scarce ships to battleships at short range. Historical command decisions need to be assessed against contemporary intelligence, mission needs, and the risk to irreplaceable assets.

evidence.note: The panel rejects a cowardice claim, weighs Fletcher's available information, and contrasts carrier air support with exposing the carriers themselves to close-range battleship attack.

segments.summary: Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher's disputed carrier decision needs to be judged against the intelligence and operational risks he faced rather than dismissed as cowardice through hindsight.

segments.title: Human-seeding stories are not evidence of real origins
segments.body: Shared science-fiction motifs do not show that humanity was settled from elsewhere. Battlestar Galactica's recurring cycle is a thematic choice rather than a historical claim. Star Trek's ancient precursor explanation supplies a storytelling reason for many aliens sharing a humanoid form. A further reference to an evolved dinosaur species reinforces that these are fictional premises assembled for narrative and production needs. Resemblance between myths or fictional settings is not evidence for human origins by itself.

evidence.note: The question links Battlestar Galactica and Star Trek to human origins, and the panel distinguishes thematic and production devices from historical evidence.

segments.question: Do recurring human-seeding stories in Battlestar Galactica and Star Trek reveal a literal truth about humanity's origins?
segments.answerShort: No. Battlestar Galactica's cycle is a theme, and Star Trek's precursor seeding is a storytelling device rather than historical evidence.

segments.title: A hidden carrier could support dispersed Rebel raids
segments.body: The absence of Venator-type carriers from the Rebel Alliance follows from how the films were created more than from an unavoidable in-universe constraint. Hyperdrive-equipped fighters could launch from a carrier held well away from the target and recover at a different rendezvous after the raid. That would conceal the carrier's position and make attacks appear from unpredictable directions. Imperial interdictors could counter the scheme by restricting the mobility on which it depends. The fictional plan applies distributed basing and operational reach while denying the enemy a clear trail back to supporting assets.

evidence.note: The panel proposes remote Venator basing, hyperdrive raids, changing recovery points, and Imperial interdictors as a counter.

segments.summary: Star Wars hyperdrives could let fighters launch from a carrier in one system and recover in another, frustrating Imperial efforts to locate their base.

segments.title: A sector fleet needs escorts as well as capital ships
segments.body: An Imperial sector force built around capital ships alone would leave routine missions uncovered. Smaller escorts are needed for jobs that fictional stories often assign to a Star Destroyer, such as pursuing a corvette. The historical analogy is that an escort force can be numerous yet still inadequate for the tasks expected of it. Combat power includes the ships that screen, patrol, and handle dispersed demands as well as the largest hulls.

evidence.note: The answer calls for more smaller escorts and explains why capital ships alone are an unbalanced fleet.

segments.question: What would a more realistic Imperial Navy sector fleet require?
segments.answerShort: Keep major capital ships and add many more corvettes, cruisers, and other escort assets so heavy units are not misused for routine local tasks.

segments.title: Real US warships behind an Azur Lane anniversary wish list
segments.body: A game roster question opens a tour of distinctive US Navy candidates. USS Albany is proposed in her guided-missile conversion, offering a ship unlike another conventional gun cruiser or carrier. USS England is raised for her anti-submarine record, while Des Moines, Alaska, the Iowa class, and further Essex-class carriers supply other historically recognisable choices. A large existing Essex roster makes another sister possible but less novel. These candidates connect fictionalised game characters with the real ships and design histories behind them.

evidence.note: The panel considers Albany, Des Moines, England, Alaska, Iowa-class battleships, and Essex-class carriers for an Azur Lane event.

segments.question: Which US-faction ships would make strong additions to Azur Lane's anniversary event?
segments.answerShort: The suggestions range from the converted missile cruiser USS Albany and the Des Moines class to USS England, Alaska, additional Iowa-class battleships, and another Essex-class carrier.

segments.title: UNSC ship choices reveal different fleet-design priorities
segments.body: No single fictional ship dominates because the choices optimise different capabilities. Infinity is attractive partly because its parasite escorts turn one acquisition into a small force, and the Punic-class supercarrier offers a similar package with carried Paris-class frigates. Other answers favour specialised stealth hulls such as Point Blank and related prowler designs. True invisibility also differs from sensor dampening, electronic countermeasures, and low-visibility coatings. Although the technology belongs to Halo, the comparison exposes familiar tradeoffs among concentrated capacity, organic escorts, intelligence access, and survivability.

evidence.note: The panel compares Infinity, Punic-class carriers, embedded escorts, prowlers, Point Blank, sensor dampening, and visual concealment.

segments.question: Which UNSC warship would each panel member most like to own?
segments.answerShort: Large carriers such as Infinity and the Punic class win support for their embedded escorts, while stealth ships such as Point Blank appeal for infiltration and intelligence work.

segments.title: Andromeda needed to use its industrial and political premise
segments.body: Later seasons narrowed too much around Dylan Hunt and neglected the ensemble and the ship's unusual capabilities. Andromeda could reportedly rebuild much of herself from asteroid resources, making her an industrial base as well as a warship. The series rarely followed through on what that capacity meant for logistics, recovery, or rebuilding a fleet. Its largest structural problem is the move from a roaming ship to a fledgling Systems Commonwealth whose scale, authority, and relationship to Andromeda remain unclear. Acquiring a government changes command, resources, and obligations, and the story needed to account for that transition.

evidence.note: The panel discusses Dylan Hunt, Andromeda's rebuilding capacity, asteroid resources, and the mishandled transition to a restored Commonwealth.

segments.question: What should change if Andromeda were remade as a stronger television series?
segments.answerShort: Reduce the show's concentration on Dylan Hunt, make more of Andromeda's self-repair and production capacity, and handle the transition from lone ship to restored Commonwealth coherently.

segments.title: Gloire and Monitor show why seakeeping changes a matchup
segments.body: A Gloire-versus-Monitor encounter is less lopsided than a comparison with the faster HMS Warrior. Monitor might be able to catch Gloire, so speed alone does not decide the hypothetical engagement. Gloire can operate in open water that would be dangerous for the low-freeboard American monitor. She could therefore refuse combat by remaining beyond Monitor's safe operating environment. Tactical performance depends on seakeeping and the geography in which a ship can actually fight.

evidence.note: The panel contrasts Warrior's speed with Gloire and explains how Gloire could use open-sea conditions that Monitor could not tolerate.

segments.summary: A counterfactual comparison notes that Monitor might catch the slower Gloire, yet Gloire could remain offshore where the low-freeboard monitor could not safely follow.

segments.title: French intervention could widen the Russo-Japanese War
segments.body: French intervention on Russia's side is treated as a counterfactual rather than an account of the actual war. The Anglo-Japanese Alliance would make British involvement likely, and Royal Navy control of European exits could stop Russian and French reinforcements from reaching the Far East. Germany, Italy, and Austria-Hungary might then exploit the alignment by joining Britain and Japan. That possibility would turn an East Asian conflict into a much wider European confrontation. Alliance obligations and maritime access can matter more than the paper strength of a fleet that cannot reach the theatre.

evidence.note: The panel explores a French intervention counterfactual, the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, blocked fleet routes, and possible European alignments.

segments.summary: In a counterfactual where France joins Russia, the Anglo-Japanese Alliance could draw Britain in and prevent French or Russian fleets from reaching East Asia.

segments.title: Why larger guns are not a simple battleship refit
segments.body: A physically possible refit may still be a poor modernization. Installing a larger weapon would require a new turret and substantial work below it. The Wyoming layout may also force a loss of guns because some superfiring positions are narrower than others. Even where the machinery can be made to fit, the resulting ship could be expensive, maintenance-heavy, and less useful than a cleaner design solution.

evidence.note: The panel weighs barbette dimensions, replacement turrets, expense, and the practical value of a 14-inch conversion.

segments.question: Could the Wyoming or Rivadavia classes have been refitted with 14-inch guns?
segments.answerShort: Their barbettes may offer theoretical room, but new turrets, uneven barbette dimensions, cost, maintenance, and lost guns make the conversion unattractive.

segments.title: Pre-war mechanised loading is not modern automation
segments.body: A pre-war autoloader would use highly mechanised loading rather than modern autonomous control. Relays, switches, mechanical computers, and carefully sequenced human work could reduce a very large gun crew, though the machinery would take considerable space and remain vulnerable to shock. Raising a ten-gun broadside from roughly two to five rounds per minute would radically alter its apparent firepower. The same automation label can therefore conceal very different staffing, reliability, and control arrangements.

evidence.note: The answer distinguishes relay-based mechanisation from modern sensing and explains rate-of-fire and crew implications.

segments.question: How disruptive would a Vickers battleship-calibre autoloader be before the First World War?
segments.answerShort: A system raising heavy-gun fire to four or five rounds per minute would alarm rival navies, but it would be relay-and-mechanism control rather than the sensor-rich automation of today.

segments.title: Choosing a German warship to preserve
segments.body: Allowing both completed ships and unfinished projects creates a choice between preservation value and design curiosity. Gneisenau with 15-inch guns is chosen as a powerful and politically conspicuous surviving battleship. Praise for Graf Zeppelin is deliberately sarcastic and criticises the German carrier programme. Other suggestions stretch the rules toward captured or incomplete hulls to settle arguments about what those designs might really have become. The choices separate a desire for an effective ship from interest in a physical case study of a troubled design.

evidence.note: The panel considers Gneisenau with 15-inch guns, sarcastically nominates Graf Zeppelin, and explores incomplete or captured hulls under the question's rules.

segments.question: Which German warship from either world war would be the most interesting to own if an incomplete ship were delivered complete?
segments.answerShort: The clearest serious choice is Gneisenau completed with 15-inch guns, while Graf Zeppelin is offered sarcastically as a way to expose the carrier design's flaws.

segments.title: Game balance is not the same as historical performance
segments.body: Gaming balance and historical performance answer different needs. A game usually needs comparable chances across technology tiers and a ruleset in which a player's early mistake does not make the entire match pointless. Historical ships and institutions were never designed to provide that kind of fairness. Their in-game statistics can be useful mechanics without providing reliable evidence for actual capability. Balance decisions should therefore stay out of naval-history claims.

evidence.note: The panel distinguishes gaming reality from historical reality and explains the need for fair technology tiers and recoverable player mistakes.

segments.summary: A short aside explains why a game may alter ship performance to provide fair progression and prevent one mistake from making a player's position hopeless.

segments.title: Wave-motion weapons change an Imperial fleet matchup
segments.body: The science-fiction spacecraft borrows the historical battleship's form, although their capabilities are unrelated. Comparing its antimatter and wave-motion weapons with Star Wars shields and turbolasers requires assumptions that cannot be proved across settings. A Yamato firing its main weapon must recharge its shield and temporarily loses some mobility, creating a window an opponent could exploit. Operating several ships together reduces that vulnerability because one vessel can cover another. Stronger Imperial fighter numbers and attritional attacks also make force employment as important as a single dramatic weapon.

evidence.note: The panel compares fictional weapon and shield rules, wave-motion recharge limits, mutual support, Imperial fighters, and numerical attrition.

segments.question: What happens if the Rebel Alliance receives a grand fleet of Space Battleship Yamato vessels after Yavin?
segments.answerShort: Under the fictional settings' stated capabilities, wave-motion shields and guns give the Yamato force a major advantage, although recharge windows, Imperial fighters, and overwhelming numbers offer possible counters.

segments.title: New technology changes warfare without erasing its problems
segments.body: Visual-range combat is one recurring science-fiction mistake that points to a wider historical problem. New technology can modify how forces fight, improve particular capabilities, and create new constraints. It rarely erases every previous problem at once. Novelty cannot substitute for logistics, command, targeting, or sound force design.

evidence.note: The panel says new generations of technology modify and improve warfare rather than completely replacing earlier realities.

segments.question: Which science-fiction mistake makes far-future forces look as though they learned nothing from twentieth-century warfare?
segments.answerShort: Visual-range combat is one example, while the larger mistake is assuming new technology erases every earlier operational lesson instead of modifying the old problem.

segments.title: Writing space combat with manoeuvre as well as targeting
segments.body: An impeller wedge does not necessarily turn space warfare into a flat fight. Ships can preserve three-dimensional movement through corkscrewing, changes above and below a system plane, or sensor-denial constraints. The Lost Fleet explicitly places course changes above and below a system plane. At a space-warfare gathering, a German rear admiral reportedly highlighted Peacekeepers of Sol because its author had studied destroyer-flotilla tactics before projecting them into space. Authors choose rules that produce the campaign and tactical problem they want to explore. Those rules should distinguish mobility from targeting instead of using familiar naval imagery as an unexplained substitute for physics.

evidence.note: The discussion contrasts targeting with mobility, cites The Lost Fleet's three-dimensional manoeuvre, and connects Peacekeepers of Sol to research on destroyer-flotilla tactics.

segments.question: Do science-fiction settings have to force fleets into two-dimensional combat?
segments.answerShort: Usually authors restrict targeting rather than movement, and a credible setting can retain three-dimensional manoeuvre while explaining why sensors, weapons, and audience readability impose limits.

segments.title: A destroyer flotilla is shaped by maintenance availability
segments.body: A nine-ship flotilla begins with the vessels that are actually available. Newer leaders and Admiralty-pattern destroyers are preferred where possible. Ships in maintenance alter the choice, so older hulls can join when newer ones are unavailable. Readiness and repair status shape a force more than its paper order of battle.

evidence.note: The answer explains that a nine-ship flotilla is made from the vessels not in maintenance or refit.

segments.question: Which ships would form a recreated Australian Scrap Iron Flotilla?
segments.answerShort: The desired nine ships would be selected from the destroyer leader and newer destroyers, but the actual composition would depend on which hulls were in maintenance or refit.

segments.title: What early naval lasers might do against surface targets
segments.body: A laser's quoted power is only the beginning of the engineering question. A surface craft has more room to distribute systems than a small aerial drone, and the useful effect depends on where the beam hits and how rapidly it delivers heat. Thermal blooming, water, wave effects, and practical experience with the new weapon all matter. The first deployed generation may prove useful without solving every surface-target problem.

evidence.note: The panel discusses DragonFire, target space, heat delivery, atmospheric effects, and first-generation system limits.

segments.question: What is the practical limit of warship lasers against small boats and surface drones?
segments.answerShort: They may eventually defeat such targets, but early systems face energy, thermal, aim-point, atmospheric, and target-layout limits that make first-generation performance uncertain.

segments.title: Wireless power carries efficiency and safety costs
segments.body: Wireless transmission does not make power infrastructure effortless. Energy sent through the atmosphere suffers conversion and path losses, so the source must generate more than the receiver uses. An orbital microwave system also creates a concentrated beam whose misdirection could become a severe industrial accident even without a hostile actor. A cable may be inelegant, though it confines the energy to a known route and avoids many atmospheric losses. Technical possibility alone does not make a system efficient or safe to operate.

evidence.note: The panel discusses orbital microwave power, atmospheric transmission, efficiency losses, accident risk, and wired alternatives.

segments.summary: A laser discussion broadens into a warning that long-range wireless power is physically possible but loses energy and creates serious control, liability, and accident problems.

segments.title: Caribbean naval materials came through Atlantic trade
segments.body: Brass and bronze used in the Caribbean were imported from Europe rather than produced locally. Their arrival therefore depended on Atlantic shipping. This small material detail places regional naval and commercial activity within a supply network extending back to European industry. Metal availability depended on trade routes as well as local demand.

evidence.note: The panel states that Caribbean brass and bronze were imported from Europe.

segments.question: How were brass and bronze obtained in the Age of Sail Caribbean?
segments.answerShort: These materials were imported from Europe rather than produced locally at scale.

segments.title: Småland combined missiles with a torpedo attack
segments.body: Småland retained missiles and torpedoes because they served successive parts of an attack. Missiles would suppress or destroy a convoy's escorts before the destroyer closed to launch torpedoes at the merchant ships. Against a cruiser such as a Sverdlov, the sequence becomes more direct: fire the missiles, close the range, and add the torpedoes. Carrying both weapon types gives the commander options against different parts of the formation. The striking weapons fit follows from the operational sequence it was intended to support.

evidence.note: The panel describes Småland using missiles against escorts and torpedoes against a convoy, with both weapons used against a cruiser.

segments.summary: Comments on the Swedish destroyer Småland lead to an attack sequence in which missiles engage escorts before torpedoes are used against the convoy itself.

segments.title: How early could a fast ocean liner reach 27 knots?
segments.body: Mauretania and Lusitania show that liners were already approaching the mid-twenties in knots before the First World War. Bremen later held a 27-knot record, though the underlying technical possibility could have arrived earlier. Machinery, capital, and fuel costs all limited sustained speed. A company could buy greater transatlantic performance if prestige and passenger appeal justified the expenditure.

evidence.note: The answer cites Mauretania, Lusitania, Bremen, and the commercial cost of pursuing high speed.

segments.question: When did 27-knot or faster ocean liners become plausible?
segments.answerShort: The technology was practical in the 1900s and 1910s, while sustained speed depended on what an owner would pay to build and operate.

segments.title: Planning a naval-history museum trip in Australia
segments.body: The Australian National Maritime Museum is large enough to reward at least two days rather than a quick stop. Perth offers a cluster of maritime, aviation, and vehicle collections. At the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, visitors can ask staff about any legitimate opportunity to see stored collections, though access cannot be assumed. Australian holdings include a broad range of material brought home after the world wars. Together these museums offer a practical route into naval, military, and material history through surviving artefacts.

evidence.note: The panel recommends collections in Perth, Sydney, Canberra, and Brisbane and discusses the scale of Australian war holdings.

segments.question: Which Australian military and maritime museums are recommended for a multi-city trip?
segments.answerShort: Highlights include Perth's museum collections, the Australian National Maritime Museum in Sydney, and the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, while Brisbane also has a preserved frigate worth seeing.

segments.title: Magnetic armour has different combat and radiation problems
segments.body: Aligned dipoles might strengthen a fictional material's structure, though repeated energising and de-energising could leave it brittle. A magnetic field has a clearer possible role in managing charged space radiation, which is a major constraint for crewed travel. Any such protection would still need to account for plasma effects and failure modes. Fictional armour therefore remains separate from the practical problem of providing storm shelter and radiation protection for a spacecraft crew.

evidence.note: The panel considers polarisation, brittleness, plasma, and radiation protection during a Mars journey.

segments.question: What would happen if armour were magnetised or polarised?
segments.answerShort: Repeated polarisation might create materials problems, while magnetic fields may be more promising for radiation protection than as a universal answer to weapons.

segments.title: Electrical protection ideas against magnetic threats
segments.body: Electrical protection covers several ideas rather than one simple armour technology. One intended use was making it harder to attach magnetic charges or trigger magnetic detonators against a ship. Some armoured vehicles could also pass current through their protection to drive people away from the hull. Each method targets the interaction between a weapon's trigger, the platform, and its operating environment.

evidence.note: The panel discusses high-voltage armour, magnetic charges and detonators, and electrified vehicle protection.

segments.question: Did British forces develop high-voltage protection to defeat magnetic threats?
segments.answerShort: Electrical protection could disrupt magnetic charges or detonators on ships or pass current through vehicle protection to deter close attackers.

segments.title: Historical names give a fictional warship a character
segments.body: The naming question mixes Warhammer 40,000 convention with real naval memory. Ashanti is selected for the Royal Navy destroyer's repeated survival of attacks during the Second World War, giving the fictional ship a symbolic form of luck. Other answers include Dauntless and deliberately grandiose titles suited to an Overlord-class battlecruiser. Names can signal endurance, institutional lineage, or political ambition before a ship ever appears in action. That inherited meaning explains why navies and naval fiction reuse names with an established history.

evidence.note: The panel proposes Ashanti, Dominion Authority, and Dauntless and explains the historical survival association behind Ashanti.

segments.question: What names would suit a newly commanded Imperial Overlord-class ship, and why?
segments.answerShort: Ashanti is chosen for the historical destroyer's reputation for surviving wartime danger, while Dauntless and grander fictional names offer different traditions.

segments.title: Why fast ocean liners largely lost their market
segments.body: Queen Mary 2 shows how rare the remaining ocean-liner niche has become. Historical fast liners were designed around transport and schedule, with fewer of the accommodations and attractions expected of a modern cruise ship. They also cannot compete with aircraft for crossing time. A vessel type can remain culturally attractive after losing the economic conditions that once made it a mainstream service.

evidence.note: The discussion compares Queen Mary 2, cruise amenities, and transoceanic aircraft competition.

segments.question: Could fast ocean liners still work as modern historical cruise ships?
segments.answerShort: They face a narrow market because they offer fewer cruise amenities than modern liners and are much slower than long-haul aircraft.

segments.title: Extreme speed does not eliminate the need for protection
segments.body: Avoiding a hit is valuable, but speed alone does not make a spacecraft safe. A ball bearing or cloud of shot encountered at a high fraction of light speed becomes a high-energy impact. The threat comes from relative velocity, so an object that is trivial at ordinary speed can be destructive in this setting. Protection, avoidance, and route control therefore remain part of the design problem. A new performance advantage often creates a new exposure instead of removing every old one.

evidence.note: The panel discusses speed, armour, scattered shot, ball bearings, and the energy of impacts at a high fraction of light speed.

segments.summary: A very fast spacecraft still needs protection because even small debris or deliberately scattered shot carries enormous relative energy at a substantial fraction of light speed.

segments.title: What related warship designs would share
segments.body: Propulsion and fire control are the most likely systems to be shared between contemporaneous armoured-cruiser and battlecruiser projects. Engines would provide the main shared machinery, while fire-control equipment could transfer across both designs. Some additional overlap is possible, though it would be limited. Related projects could therefore reuse key technology without making their wider designs interchangeable.

evidence.note: The answer identifies engines and fire control as the main expected shared technology.

segments.question: How much technology would a large 9.2-inch armoured cruiser share with an Invincible-class battlecruiser?
segments.answerShort: The designs would share engines and fire control, with relatively limited interchange beyond those major systems.

segments.title: Why Yamato handled shells vertically
segments.body: A vertical shell route can reduce the size of the opening through protected structure. Large shells also tend to be stored vertically, making that handling path a coherent layout choice. British and American practice favoured conversion lower in the ship because designers judged it safer. The different arrangements reflect distinct assessments of protection, storage, and risk rather than one universally superior method.

evidence.note: The panel contrasts Japanese vertical shell handling with British and American conversion arrangements.

segments.question: Why did Yamato's shell elevators handle shells vertically rather than like British and American systems?
segments.answerShort: The Japanese arrangement sought a smaller break through armour and fitted its preferred shell-storage approach, while British and American systems made the conversion lower down for safety.

segments.title: Judging science fiction by plot, setting, and engineering
segments.body: The answers use different criteria instead of forming an objective league table. Iron Sky is criticised for plot holes, Stargate is offered as a favourite, and pre-Disney Star Wars is praised for a lived-in setting whose machinery and infrastructure remain visible. Star Trek divides opinion between its television and film forms, with individual strong films separated from uneven franchise-level judgments. Thunderbirds draws criticism for unnecessarily complicated launch engineering even from speakers who appreciate parts of its vehicle design. Technical plausibility, character development, world-building, and personal nostalgia lead to different evaluations of the same work.

evidence.note: The panel compares Iron Sky, Stargate, Star Trek, Star Wars, and Thunderbirds while debating plot, setting, engineering, and nostalgia.

segments.question: What does each panel member consider the best and worst science-fiction series?
segments.answerShort: There is no common ranking because the answers apply different standards to plot, world-building, engineering, nostalgia, and format across Stargate, Star Wars, Star Trek, Iron Sky, and Thunderbirds.

segments.title: Medium-speed diesels trade compactness for flexibility
segments.body: Medium-speed diesels are technically possible, particularly when they produce electrical power rather than driving shafts directly. The price is space because more or smaller engines have to be distributed through the hull. That changes subdivision, weight, fuel use, and oil requirements. The choice is a procurement tradeoff between a compact specialised plant and a more available, space-hungry alternative.

evidence.note: The answer addresses medium-speed diesels, generator use, hull space, subdivision, fuel, and oil.

segments.question: Could medium-speed diesels replace scarce high-speed engines in a modern frigate?
segments.answerShort: Yes, especially as generator sets, but they need more hull volume, subdivision, and attention to fuel and lubrication demands.

segments.title: An elderly Beatty would be kept in a policy role
segments.body: Age matters more here than Beatty's First World War command record. By 1939 he would have been far too old for the demands of active fleet command. The suggested outcome is a safe policy or advisory role in Britain, well away from active operations. Such an appointment would keep him out of an operational command that required a younger officer.

evidence.note: The panel says an elderly Beatty would receive a safe policy role in Britain away from operations.

segments.question: What role might David Beatty have received if he were still alive when the Second World War began?
segments.answerShort: Beatty would probably receive a safe policy or advisory post in Britain, well away from operational command, because of his age.

segments.title: A fictional fleet is constrained by its rarest component
segments.body: Procurement economics drives this fictional fleet problem. Independent planets can afford sublight gunboats more readily than interstellar warships, and rare class-one drive components form the real production bottleneck. Building a smaller FTL ship does not save the scarce component, so it produces less useful capacity for nearly the same critical cost. A proposed group of coupled craft also creates a redundancy trap because losing one member can prevent its partners from forming a viable field. An effective design has to optimise around the limiting industrial resource instead of the platform's most visible feature.

evidence.note: The panel discusses independent-world budgets, gunboats, rare FTL components, maximum-volume hulls, coupled fields, and redundancy failures.

segments.question: How could a disloyal planner build a deliberately bad fleet for an independent world in the Castle Federation setting?
segments.answerShort: Waste the planet's economy on an inefficient FTL capital ship or small craft whose expensive drive components, poor redundancy, and coupled operation erase the supposed savings.

segments.title: Could rocket recovery become a naval support mission?
segments.body: A vessel could hold position or manoeuvre in an ocean recovery area while a rocket returns. Such a platform could bring landing, maintenance, and launch-support systems together, using beacons and tracking equipment to manage the approach. Its cost and complexity would make reliable tracking and redundancy important. An asset operating in international waters would also create a protection and security problem alongside the engineering work.

evidence.note: The panel considers a sea-based rocket retrieval, maintenance, and launch platform with tracking redundancy.

segments.question: Could specialist vessels retrieve and support reusable rockets at sea?
segments.answerShort: A ship could combine recovery, maintenance, launch support, beacons, tracking, and redundancy, but it would be large, complex, and valuable enough to need protection.

segments.title: Destroying communications can unravel an interstellar state
segments.body: In the Castle Federation setting, the defeated polity begins to unravel after a coordinated strike destroys every quantum-entanglement communications relay. Isolated member worlds retain local governments, while the federal centre loses the infrastructure needed to coordinate them. A military leader then avoids accountability, seizes the legislature, and uses it as a rubber stamp while ordering the fleet and communications network rebuilt. Roman precedents help describe a system held together by coercive force instead of restored legitimacy. When that leader dies, the structure loses its principal source of unity. Communications infrastructure, institutional consent, and state capacity all become operational vulnerabilities.

evidence.note: The panel describes destroyed quantum-entanglement relays, isolated member worlds, a military seizure of the legislature, coerced unity, and renewed fragmentation after the ruler's death.

segments.summary: A Castle Federation tangent shows how a coordinated strike on quantum-communications relays can fragment a polity and create space for military rule.

segments.title: BattleTech warships expose armour and mission-design problems
segments.body: BattleTech's naval problem cannot be solved by making every warship subordinate to BattleMechs. Early ship designs are criticised for inadequate armour and defensive batteries too weak to look credible against fighters. The setting also gives large warships a powerful operational advantage: they can bombard from well beyond a planet while moving enough to frustrate limited-range strike craft. Fighters remain useful against targets near their own scale, such as dropships, without replacing capital ships. Within BattleTech's rules, the comparison tests protection, range, and mission alignment in force design.

evidence.note: The panel discusses BattleTech FTL limits, armour, anti-fighter weapons, Succession War losses, standoff bombardment, and strike-craft limits.

segments.question: How could BattleTech's space-navy element work better with its BattleMech-centred setting?
segments.answerShort: The designs need stronger protection and anti-fighter weapons while preserving the setting's FTL bottleneck and the warships' ability to bombard beyond ordinary strike-craft reach.

segments.title: Operation Crusader and the cost of mechanical unreliability
segments.body: Operation Crusader challenges an overconfident view of armoured force availability. A formation can lose a large share of its usable strength to mechanical defects before the enemy destroys it. Reliability, recovery, and maintenance are therefore part of combat power rather than background administration. The desert campaign provides a practical comparison for fictional force-design claims.

evidence.note: The panel cites Operation Crusader and notes that mechanical defects could account for very heavy tank losses.

segments.summary: A comparison with BattleTech leads to a historical reminder that Allied tank losses in Operation Crusader could stem from mechanical failure as well as enemy action.

segments.title: Fictional technologies ranked by real-world payoff
segments.body: Asteroid mining receives the broadest economic significance because access to off-world resources could change terrestrial supply and prices. Coupling extraction to an industrial base in space would matter more than returning raw material alone. Other answers prioritise medical advances and brain-computer interfaces for their direct human benefits. Matter fabricators are valued as versatile engineering tools, while power armour and fictional marine enhancements are more specialised choices. Some technologies could reshape an entire economy, while others offer a powerful but narrower capability.

evidence.note: The panel chooses asteroid mining, space industry, medical technology, brain-computer interfaces, power armour, enhancements, and matter fabricators.

segments.question: Which technologies from Glynn Stewart's science-fiction settings would be most valuable in reality?
segments.answerShort: Asteroid mining and space industry lead the economic choices, while medical technology, brain-computer interfaces, matter fabricators, power armour, and human enhancements appeal for other uses.

segments.title: First contact exposes the head-of-state distinction
segments.body: The hypothetical turns on constitutional roles rather than a search for the most powerful politician. For a formal British introduction in 2026, King Charles is the enduring head of state. In the United States, the president combines the roles of head of state and head of the executive government. The Speaker of the House leads a legislative chamber and is therefore not an equivalent national representative. Diplomatic protocol depends on constitutional structure as well as political influence.

evidence.note: The panel distinguishes the UK monarch and prime minister from the US president and the legislative role of the Speaker of the House.

segments.question: If aliens asked to be taken to Earth's leader in 2026, whom should they approach?
segments.answerShort: There is no single world leader: in the United Kingdom the monarch is head of state and the prime minister heads government, while the US president combines those constitutional roles.

segments.title: Thunderbirds needs conventional launch infrastructure
segments.body: The launch infrastructure causes the largest engineering problems in Thunderbirds. A rocket produces a thermal and radiological signature that cannot realistically be hidden by sending it through a resort building or a moving pool. Conventional launch pads and clear blast zones would avoid hardening unnecessary structures and exposing them to exhaust. Electromagnetic acceleration could provide a science-fiction aid without requiring a maze of mechanical scenery. Support infrastructure should follow the demands of heat, clearance, maintenance, and safety.

evidence.note: The panel proposes conventional launch facilities, discusses thermal and radiation signatures, blast clearance, hardened structures, and electromagnetic assistance.

segments.question: How could the engineering of the Thunderbirds vehicles and base be improved?
segments.answerShort: Retain the useful airframes and replace elaborate concealed launch routes with conventional pads, runways, clearance zones, and possibly electromagnetic launch assistance.

segments.title: Why the X-wing wins a fictional fighter comparison
segments.body: Visual appeal and operational usefulness produce different choices. Babylon 5's Starfury is admired, while the X-wing's shields, integrated life support, and hyperdrive make it far more independent of a carrier or local base. Limited familiarity with Space: Above and Beyond's Hammerhead prevents a firm comparison, and some speakers prefer different fictional craft altogether. The answers do not form a universal performance ranking. Protection, crew support, and strategic mobility can outweigh appearance when selecting a small combat spacecraft.

evidence.note: The panel compares the Starfury, X-wing, and Hammerhead, favouring the X-wing's shields, life support, and hyperdrive while noting personal preferences and limited familiarity.

segments.question: Which fighter offers the strongest choice: a Starfury, an X-wing, or a Hammerhead?
segments.answerShort: Most choose the X-wing because shields, integrated life support, and a hyperdrive give it the broadest self-contained capability, even when other craft are preferred aesthetically.

segments.title: A late-built BC-304 could inherit mature technology
segments.body: The fictional name draws on a famously durable Royal Navy battleship. Building the BC-304 after Asgard technology transfer would allow sensors, weapons, and other systems to be incorporated into the design instead of added piecemeal. Later customers sometimes avoid the failures suffered by the first ships while still receiving the improved equipment. Early operators gain capability sooner while exposing their hulls to the initial battles and design defects. The scenario captures a real procurement tension between early access and technological maturity.

evidence.note: The panel discusses a British BC-304 named Warspite, built-in Asgard upgrades, order timing, early losses, and the benefit of receiving a later corrected design.

segments.question: What would a British BC-304 named HMS Warspite look like if Asgard upgrades were incorporated from the start?
segments.answerShort: It would be an unusually formidable late-production ship, benefiting from systems already integrated and corrected rather than receiving the earliest, least mature version of the design.

segments.title: A mixed task force needs sensors and a flag command post
segments.body: Each fictional class receives a distinct job. Sovereigns provide the heaviest combat power, Intrepids offer a strong long-range sensor picture, and Akiras and Defiants add concentrated offensive capability. Danube craft with torpedo pods broaden the number of firing units, while proposed Typhon or Nebula additions would improve command or support. Command would work best from the strongest information node, though an ordinary Intrepid bridge lacks space for an admiral's staff. A balanced force also needs a flag command post able to turn specialised reports and weapons into one plan.

evidence.note: The panel assigns roles to Sovereign, Akira, Intrepid, Defiant, and Danube vessels and discusses sensors, Typhons, staff space, and a flag bridge.

segments.question: How dangerous would a Dominion War task force of Sovereign, Akira, Intrepid, Defiant, and Danube-class vessels be?
segments.answerShort: Very dangerous: its heavy ships, torpedo platforms, scouts, and small combatants cover complementary roles, though the commander still needs a proper flag bridge and staff.

segments.title: A Lucrehulk could give Skynet an interstellar industrial base
segments.body: The premise pits two fictional rule sets against each other. A Lucrehulk supplies droids, industrial equipment, and access to interstellar systems that a victorious Skynet does not possess on its own. The key constraint is whether Skynet can reconstruct the wider FTL communications network from the ship's equipment. If it can, its established ability to hide and deceive would let it build quietly from asteroid resources before revealing a hybrid fleet. Appearing during the breakdown of Clone Wars command structures could also undermine Palpatine's control of both sides, making timing and deception as important as the machines themselves.

evidence.note: The panel discusses Lucrehulk droids and production, FTL communications, asteroid mining, Skynet concealment, and strategic timing around the Clone Wars.

segments.question: How would Terminator's Skynet use a crashed Lucrehulk around the time of Star Wars Episode I?
segments.answerShort: It could absorb droid, FTL, communications, and production technology, hide while mining asteroids, and emerge as a machine fleet at a politically disruptive moment.

segments.title: Fast minelayers would face a predictable Tobruk route
segments.body: The Abdiels could run quickly into and out of Tobruk. Speed, however, does not remove the danger of a repeated supply route whose destination and approach are known to the enemy. Mines can be laid in advance without an opposing force waiting for the ship at the moment of passage. Committing a fast minelayer also diverts a scarce asset from other missions that exploit its unusual capability. Rapid delivery therefore has to be balanced against route clearance, predictability, and opportunity cost.

evidence.note: The panel weighs Abdiel-class speed against scarcity, a predictable destination, pre-laid mines, and the need to sweep the route.

segments.question: How useful would Abdiel-class fast minelayers have been on the Tobruk Ferry Service?
segments.answerShort: Their speed would make them useful transports, but the route's predictability would expose scarce, capable ships to mines and require careful sweeping.

segments.title: Perfect communications would not erase Japan's resource deficit
segments.body: The counterfactual grants Japan communications that opponents cannot interrupt or intercept. That would improve the coordination of dispersed forces and remove a major source of Allied intelligence. It would not create additional fuel, ships, aircraft, trained personnel, or replacement capacity. The result would be a more difficult and possibly longer war of attrition rather than a decisive Japanese victory. Command efficiency cannot replace the material capacity needed to sustain a large industrial war.

evidence.note: The panel credits secure FTL communications with coordination and intelligence benefits but says resource disparities still decide the war.

segments.question: How would secure, instantaneous FTL communications change Japan's position in the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: They would improve coordination and deny the Allies many intercept opportunities, but they would prolong rather than reverse a war decided by overwhelming resource and industrial disparities.

segments.title: Better fighters need a system for passing on experience
segments.body: The fictional Empire receives a more capable fighter and a better personnel system. Rotating veterans into instruction prevents hard-won experience from disappearing when individual pilots are lost. Rookies would enter combat with lessons already distilled from earlier operations. The Rebellion would struggle far more against an opponent without the Empire's familiar quality and training weaknesses. Equipment and institutional learning multiply each other's effect.

evidence.note: The panel says TIE Avengers and veteran-led rookie training would make the Rebel Alliance's task far harder.

segments.question: What if the Galactic Empire replaced ordinary TIE fighters with TIE Avengers and rotated veterans into training posts?
segments.answerShort: The Rebel Alliance would face a much harder air war because better aircraft would be paired with an institution that transfers combat experience to new pilots.

segments.title: Science fiction needs more escort and screening ships
segments.body: Escort ships are the missing perspective. They carry out the screening work that gives a fleet protection and tactical awareness. Fiction often focuses on the dramatic central hull while leaving its supporting force invisible. Those supporting roles make a battle line or task group viable.

evidence.note: The panel nominates escorts and screening assets as the missing naval perspective in science fiction.

segments.question: Which underappreciated naval vessel type deserves more science-fiction attention?
segments.answerShort: Escorts and screening assets deserve the spotlight because they explain how fleets actually protect, scout for, and support their prominent heavy ships.

segments.title: A Canadian destroyer built around Burke systems
segments.body: The Arleigh Burke provides a capable baseline without supplying a design to copy unchanged. A new Canadian requirement would likely retain proven combat-system ideas while giving them a larger, more modern hull. Growth margin matters because continually adding sensors and equipment to an old form risks crowding and top-heaviness. Allied variants can adapt a common design logic to national needs without making standardisation mean uniformity.

evidence.note: The panel compares a Canadian requirement with DDG(X), Burke systems, Japanese and Korean variants, and hull growth margin.

segments.question: What might a 10,000-ton Canadian destroyer armed like an Arleigh Burke look like?
segments.answerShort: A DDG(X)-like new hull could carry Burke-style software and hardware while gaining the volume needed for modern systems.

segments.title: Convoy escort is not a stealth-only mission
segments.body: A convoy escort cannot make the whole formation invisible. Merchant ships, a carrier, and aircraft radar emissions can reveal the force before an individual frigate's signature becomes the key issue. That shifts the value calculation toward affordable, competent escort vessels instead of extreme stealth on every combatant. Present procurement efforts appear to be working up from a lower-end baseline despite institutional resistance to building such ships.

evidence.note: The panel explains why convoy and carrier-group escorts gain limited value from individual extreme stealth.

segments.question: Should the US Navy revive a low-high mix for convoy escort missions?
segments.answerShort: A simpler light frigate can make sense because an escort shares the conspicuous signature of the merchant ships or carrier group it protects, so extreme stealth is not always the decisive requirement.

segments.title: The Pentastar Alignment should consolidate before expanding
segments.body: The fictional Alignment starts in a better position than many Imperial successor regimes. It already possesses major warships, so improving quality and stability matters more than accumulating hulls without an economic base. Outreach to Thrawn or other warlords could be selective rather than an automatic move toward reunification. The Alignment should refuse a revived emperor's demand for submission and convert military control into a durable political order. Postwar state-building depends on legitimacy, revenue, and institutional survival as well as possession of capital ships.

evidence.note: The panel discusses force quality, economic strength, Super Star Destroyers, relations with warlords, resisting reunification, and creating a legitimate state.

segments.question: How should the Pentastar Alignment improve its position three years after Endor?
segments.answerShort: Strengthen the economy and force quality, secure useful capital ships and allies selectively, and resist being absorbed into a restored Empire so the Alignment can become a legitimate state.

segments.title: The Acclamator is a practical fictional strategic transport
segments.body: Practical transport depends on loading, egress, and operational use as well as internal volume. A TARDIS can hold a great deal, while its ordinary doorway creates an inconvenient bottleneck for moving a formation and its equipment. The Acclamator is a tactical and strategic lift ship that keeps troops back until the space battle is won. It can then bring the force forward quickly to secure the planet. Carrying capacity has limited value when it cannot be deployed at the required tempo.

evidence.note: The panel contrasts the TARDIS doorway with the Acclamator's role in holding troops back and rapidly deploying them after a space battle.

segments.question: What is the most practical transport vessel in science fiction, and what limits the TARDIS?
segments.answerShort: The Acclamator can hold troops safely away from a battle and then move them rapidly to a planet, while a TARDIS offers awkward access through a single small doorway.

segments.title: When an invasion force might carry surface ships
segments.body: Carried surface vessels have a role when a campaign requires access to an aquatic planet's coasts or subsurface environment. A spacefaring hull cannot simply operate underwater as well. Spacecraft are designed against outward pressure, while deep water crushes a hull inward. Basing, landing, and specialised vessel design therefore matter across these different environments.

evidence.note: The answer discusses aquatic invasions, surface vessels, subsurface operations, and the different pressure problems of space and water.

segments.question: Could large starships carry surface vessels for an invasion?
segments.answerShort: They could be useful on a largely aquatic world, but a spacecraft is not automatically a submarine because vacuum and deep-water pressure impose opposite structural demands.

segments.title: Probert's Enterprise-C design leaves the outcome unchanged
segments.body: Andrew Probert's original Enterprise-C design would change only the ship's appearance in this scene. Its intended weapons and other capabilities are treated as equivalent to the version shown. The encounter therefore unfolds the same way, and the Enterprise-C is still destroyed. The counterfactual changes the production design without changing the fictional battle.

evidence.note: The speakers say Probert's original Enterprise-C design would look different while retaining the same intended weapons, capabilities, and fate.

segments.question: What changes if the Enterprise-C uses Andrew Probert's original design?
segments.answerShort: The ship would look different while retaining the same intended weapons, capabilities, and fate.

segments.title: The recurring security dilemma behind secret services
segments.body: The fictional premise describes a recurring historical tension. States that portray themselves as humane can still rely on officials prepared to act secretly, harshly, or deceptively in the name of protection. This is the enduring 'watchers in the night' problem, connected here to covert naval assignments aimed at denying an enemy a port. The moral dilemma remains unresolved, though bureaucracy and secrecy can be powerful instruments even without open violence.

evidence.note: The panel links Section 31 with historical security services and covert naval port-denial assignments.

segments.question: How would Garak leading Section 31 affect Starfleet during the Dominion War?
segments.answerShort: Little changes structurally because the fictional organisation already reflects the historical dilemma of people using harsh methods to defend regimes that see themselves as decent.

segments.title: A family Bible preserves maritime social history
segments.body: A family Bible contains narrative entries largely maintained by women because the seafaring men supplied many of the stories but wrote poorly. Those inherited accounts serve as leads to compare with external historical records rather than unquestionable proof. One reconstructed episode follows two brothers who independently met two sisters connected with Stockholm while travelling on different voyages. The elder brother later carried the ill younger sister toward Portsmouth and Cornwall when she claimed kinship through his brother, and the pair eventually married. Ships linked distant households as well as ports, while family archives preserved social history that official naval records may not foreground. The method retains the personal account while checking names, places, and events against other evidence.

evidence.note: The panel describes women-maintained family Bible entries, cross-checking inherited accounts, two seafaring brothers, two Stockholm sisters, and a voyage toward Portsmouth and Cornwall.

segments.summary: A family anecdote shows how women-maintained Bible entries, oral memory, and external records can reconstruct relationships formed through seafaring networks.

segments.title: Expeditionary fleets need heavy and light ships
segments.body: The BC-304 is likely to remain useful, though the fictional fleet jumped to large ships without a supporting small-ship programme. A fleet needs an expeditionary asset able to carry fighters, troops, and supplies to a distant problem. It also needs patrol vessels that can maintain presence and handle lesser demands. Operating such ships in pairs could preserve capability and support across a dispersed theatre.

evidence.note: The panel calls for both a large expeditionary ship and smaller patrol and presence assets, often operating in pairs.

segments.question: What should follow the BC-304 in Stargate's ship design?
segments.answerShort: Keep a large expeditionary ship for fighters and ground forces alongside smaller patrol and presence vessels.

segments.title: Modern warships still need an offline fighting mode
segments.body: Modern ships retain the ability to function without a fully connected network. Isolation and tightly limited interfaces are central to making data systems genuinely secure. The F-35 provides an example of the concern created when many partners share interconnected systems. National customisation of command-and-control arrangements is one response to the danger of relying on an entirely generic networked architecture.

evidence.note: The panel discusses offline operation, limited interfaces, F-35 network concerns, and customised command systems.

segments.question: Could a serious AI or network compromise force modern ships totally offline?
segments.answerShort: They are prepared to operate offline, but protecting command systems requires carefully limited interfaces and continuing scrutiny of complex multinational networks.

segments.title: Separating a science-fiction work from its author's politics
segments.body: Professional defence and security work can serve democratically elected governments regardless of party. A similar distinction applies to books because an author's politics do not automatically determine whether the world-building or story is worthwhile. If the argument consumes the work, the reader may stop enjoying it. Some disagreements also have direct consequences, especially when a public position targets another person's right to live openly. Separating a work from its author is therefore a conditional judgment rather than an absolute rule.

evidence.note: The panel compares cross-party defence work with reading authors of different politics and discusses limits when politics dominate a work or target a reader's existence.

segments.question: How can readers approach science-fiction authors whose personal politics differ sharply from their own?
segments.answerShort: Judge whether the work is enjoyable and whether politics overwhelm it, while recognising that disagreement has limits when an author's position directly denies a reader's rights or existence.

segments.title: HMAS Tattoo and Australia's flexible ship-naming traditions
segments.body: A Mogami-class frigate is the tentative modern answer, while the question opens a discussion of Australian naming practice. HMAS Tattoo was an S-class destroyer despite its T-name, while Australian Daring-class ships became Vampire, Vendetta, and Voyager rather than receiving D-names. Cancelled or reassigned Royal Navy possibilities included Dervish, Decoy, Delight, Desperate, Desire, Diana, and Demon. Names changed as building plans contracted, leaving a record of ships that existed on paper but never entered service. Completing all the cited British and Australian plans would have produced twenty hulls rather than the eleven historically completed. The individual name choice connects with class identity and the force-structure consequences of a cancelled building programme.

evidence.note: The panel tentatively proposes a Mogami-class frigate for HMAS Tattoo, then discusses Australian Daring-class names, cancelled Royal Navy names, and twenty planned ships versus eleven completed hulls.

segments.question: Which twenty-first-century Australian ship class would suit the name HMAS Tattoo?
segments.answerShort: A Mogami-class frigate is the tentative choice, while earlier Australian destroyer names show that the navy has not followed a simple class-initial rule.

segments.title: The Dog Star as a naval navigational name
segments.body: HMS Dog Star draws its name from Sirius in Canis Major. The star has long been known as the Dog Star and served within the vocabulary of traditional navigation. The name therefore carries a precise astronomical and seafaring reference. What first sounds whimsical has a practical maritime association.

evidence.note: The panel explains Dog Star as Sirius in Canis Major and a traditional navigational reference.

segments.question: Why would HMS Dog Star be a serious naval name?
segments.answerShort: Dog Star is an older name for Sirius, a prominent navigational star in Canis Major, giving the name a practical maritime association.
